Learning Objectives
Describe the pathophysiology of septic arthritis in the pediatric population.
Characterize common organisms responsible for septic arthritis and associated risk factors.
Understand and apply physical examination findings, imaging studies, and diagnostic tests in
patients with septic arthritis.
Determine a treatment plan for the management of pediatric septic arthritis.
Background/Pathoanatomy
Septic arthritis is the bacteria-mediated inflammation of a joint with the potential for
destruction and degradation of cartilage and bone.
Very common in the pediatric population and closely associated with osteomyelitis
The hip and knee are the most common sites of pediatric septic arthritis.

Metaphyseal blood flow in the pediatric population is altered with sinusoids that impair and
slow blood flow and increase the susceptibility for osteomyelitis and subsequent septic
arthritis.
Septic arthritis most commonly results from adjacent osteomyelitis, hematogenous seeding of
joints, and self-decompression of abscess within the joint capsule.
Joints with intra-articular metaphyses, such as the shoulder, ankle, hip, and elbow, are at
higher risk for septic arthritis.
The mechanism of joint destruction is primarily caused by proteolytic enzyme release from
white blood cells in the presence of bacteria.

Background/Pathoanatomy
Septic arthritis is the bacteria-mediated inflammation of a joint. Although septic arthritis
also is observed in adults, it is a major problem in the pediatric population given its
increased incidence and risk of long-term complications with potential for cartilage
damage. Septic arthritis does not appear to have a predilection for sex, race, or
socioeconomic status. Children younger than 5 years account for 75% of septic arthritis
cases and appear particularly vulnerable. Various risk factors are associated with septic
arthritis, and specific organisms often are linked with certain age groups and
comorbidities.
Septic arthritis can develop via direct inoculation of a joint, hematogenous seeding, or
progression of adjacent osteomyelitis. Although the pathophysiology is not completely
understood, the overall susceptibility of the pediatric population to septic arthritis is
primarily based on the unique intraosseous vascular anatomy of the growing child and
the predilection for osteomyelitis. Vascular transphyseal channels are present in
newborns, and studies have theorized that direct hematogenous seeding of bacteria can
occur via this mechanism. These transphyseal vessels directly connect the metaphyseal
vasculature to the intra-articular epiphysis and are thought to remain open until age 18
months. This may explain the increased incidence of septic arthritis in this young
population. The bony metaphysis in children contains sinusoids, hairpin turn vascular
networks, that create a relative slowing of blood flow. This sluggish blood flow may lead
to increased potential for bacterial organisms to exit the vascular channels and adhere

to, and propagate within, the metaphysis. If osteomyelitis develops, bacteria can be
introduced into the joint via intraosseous or subperiosteal abscess formation and
subsequent decompression into the joint or via migration within transphyseal vessels.
Although septic arthritis can occur in any joint, some joints are much more commonly
affected. The hip and knee are the most frequently involved joints, composing almost
two-thirds of pediatric septic arthritis cases. Multiple joints may be affected concurrently,
a finding noted in approximately 5% of patients.1 Several joints have intra-articular
metaphyses and are, therefore, more prone to septic arthritis because the sinusoidal
network that predisposes to osteomyelitis already is encapsulated in the joint and
transphyseal seeding is not required.2 These intra-articular metaphyseal joints include
the proximal femur, proximal humerus, distal fibula, and proximal radius.
A mnemonic for joints with intra-articular metaphyses is “Septic Arthritis Hurts
Epiphyses,” with the first letter representing the joints: shoulder, ankle, hip, elbow,
respectively.
The bacteria-mediated joint destruction in patients with septic arthritis can happen
acutely and is the primary reason it is considered a surgical emergency in the pediatric
population. Although macroscopic cartilage injury may not be observed, basic science
studies have proposed that the host polymorphonuclear response and subsequent
release of proteolytic enzymes may lead to permanent destruction of intra-articular
cartilage and subchondral bone loss in as few as 3 days.3 The mechanism by which
cartilage and bone destruction occurs is a combination of the bacterial toxins and the
immune response, which may vary based on the offending organism. Proteolytic
enzymes, matrix metalloproteinases, are produced and released by activated
neutrophils during the initial inflammatory response to septic arthritis and are the
primary cause of hyaline cartilage destruction. These enzymes, along with vascular
damage, also are responsible for physeal damage. In some patients, osteonecrosis may
result from increased intracapsular pressure, creating a tamponade effect and
diminishing epiphyseal blood flow (Figure 1).

Organisms
Staphylococcus aureus is the most common causative organism in patients with septic arthritis,
regardless of age.
S aureus infection may be associated with complications, such as deep vein thrombosis,
through unique virulence factors.
Neonates, younger than 12 months, are more susceptible to group B Streptococcus.
Haemophilus influenzae and Kingella kingae are common in children aged 6 months to 5 years,
with Kingella being the primary source of culture-negative septic arthritis.

Gonococcal septic arthritis is associated with the sexually active population older than 12 years
and requires a high index of suspicion with frequent negative Gram stains.
Salmonella may be associated with sickle cell disease; however, S aureus is the most common
causative organism.
Group A Streptococcus may be associated with preceding varicella infections.
Lyme disease may cause acellular monoarthritis and is most common in patients in the
northeast region of the United States.

Organisms
S aureus, a gram-positive cocci, is the most common organism observed in pediatric
patients with septic arthritis. Although bacterial species are associated with certain ages
and comorbidities, S aureus remains the most likely organism regardless of age.4
Regardless, surgeons must be familiar with the organisms associated with specific age
ranges. The neonatal population, particularly those who have never left the hospital,
often are more susceptible to group B Streptococcus (S agalactiae) and other nosocomial
organisms given the use of invasive lines and catheters during the first weeks of life.
Younger patients (1 to 5 years) have historically been linked with H influenzae septic
arthritis. This incidence has decreased as a result of vaccinations but may still be
observed. Infection with H influenzae also has been associated with meningitis and may
require additional workup via lumbar puncture. As cases of H influenzae have decreased,
septic arthritis caused by K kingae, an anaerobic gram-negative bacillus, has increased.
This bacterium is more challenging to culture and can be better isolated with growth in
blood culture medium or with isolation via polymerase chain reaction.5Because of the
low rate of positive cultures in patients with normal laboratory studies, many children
are deemed culture-negative, with rates varying from 21% to 70% in large case series.
The use of polymerase chain reaction has resulted in a considerable rise in cases of
Kingella septic arthritis, which may prove that Kingella is the primary pathogen in many
patients, possibly outnumbering S aureus in patients younger than 2 years.6 Neisseria
gonorrhoeae, a gram-negative diplococci, may be a source of septic and nonbacterial
arthritis in sexually active individuals, typically older than 12 years. This organism may be
difficult to identify and often does not yield a positive culture. Its presentation may be
associated with polyarthralgia; therefore, a high index of suspicion should be maintained

to select the correct laboratory evaluation and subsequent treatment options. Infections
associated with N gonorrhoeae do not always require surgical management and can be
managed via antibiotic agents alone. Gonococcal infections in the pediatric population
may be associated with child abuse, and patients should be worked up appropriately, if
indicated. Other organisms that are associated with septic arthritis, osteomyelitis, and
arthralgias are not specific to age but to other illnesses. Salmonella species infections are
more common in patients with sickle cell disease. Group A streptococcal infections may
be observed after infection with varicella. Monoarthralgias that present similar to septic
arthritis may be associated with the spirochete Borrelia burgdorferi, the causative
organism in Lyme disease. This organism must be high on the differential diagnosis in
endemic areas or in patients with certain histories of travel and tick bites. Despite these
increased frequencies in certain situations, the most common organism in all age groups
and all medical comorbidities is S aureus. Infections caused by S aureus, both methicillin-
sensitive and methicillin-resistant S aureus, have been linked to an increased incidence
of complications, including deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary infections. This is
because of unique virulence factors, such as Panton-Valentine leukocidin, which is
produced by certain strains regardless of methicillin sensitivity7(Table 1).

Presentation
Children with septic arthritis are more likely to appear toxic than patients with osteomyelitis or
other arthralgias.
Many children will present with fever, refusal to move the joint, and inability to bear weight.
Patients often will have a history of recent bacterial infection or minor trauma.
Pain at the associated joint will be severe, and children will adopt body positions to limit pain,
such as flexion, abduction, and external rotation, and to decrease intracapsular pressure in
the hip.

Presentation
Septic arthritis is a condition with the potential for considerable morbidity and requires
prompt diagnosis and management. In the pediatric population, diagnosis may be
difficult because of inability of the patient to articulate complaints and follow physical
examination requests. Therefore, a careful and detailed patient history and physical
examination are vital to ensure correct diagnosis and proper management. Most
children will present with a painful joint. In the neonatal inpatient population, septic
arthritis may present as pseudoparalysis and may be multifocal. In the community
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:08 PM
AAOS | Septic Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001052
7/25

population, initial presentation often is in the emergency department because septic
arthritis generally is acute and debilitating. Occasionally, a child with septic arthritis may
present to an outpatient clinic; therefore, a high index of suspicion must be maintained
in a young patient with these signs regardless of treatment setting. Children with septic
arthritis often appear toxic. They do not act like themselves and generally feel or appear
sick. In nonverbal children, poor feeding or increased fussiness and irritability may be
the presenting complaint. Initial vital signs often reveal a fever. A child with septic
arthritis usually will have a limp or be unable to bear weight on the affected limb. They
also will have pain with short arc movements on physical examination. Just moving the
bed a patient is lying on may elicit pain because it moves the joint. The joint itself may
appear red, hot, and swollen. Often, recent minor trauma to the affected limb is
reported. This may be coincidental but also may be a mechanism of focal injury and
inflammation, which may set the stage for infection during a period of bacteremia. A
history of recent illness may be very important. Septic arthritis often is associated with a
previous bacterial infection. This infection may be the source of hematogenous spread
to septic arthritis. This is in contrast to a previous viral infection, which may be related to
subsequent transient synovitis. Evaluation of the child as a whole rather than focusing
on the reported site of pain is important. Septic arthritis of the hip may masquerade as
knee pain given the sensory nerve distribution of the anterior branch of the obturator
nerve. With involvement of the hip, children may adopt a position of obligate flexion,
abduction, and external rotation. This maximizes joint capsule volume available if an
effusion is present. Any attempt to move the hip via the log roll maneuver, extension, or
internal rotation may elicit pain (Figures 2 and 3).

Differential Diagnosis
A child who presents with a painful joint is not an uncommon scenario. The patient
history and physical examination may help narrow the diagnosis, and the possible
etiology can be further refined via imaging and laboratory studies. Many disease
processes may mimic septic arthritis, and a good differential diagnosis list is essential.
Pediatric septic arthritis of the hip, in particular, may be associated with signs and
symptoms similar to those associated with several other pathologies. Transient synovitis
of the hip, also called toxic synovitis, is the most common cause of hip pain in school-age
children8 This process is a benign, typically postviral, inflammation of the hip synovium
and generally is self-limited. Imaging studies may reveal an effusion similar to septic
arthritis. In general, children with transient synovitis will not have as severe findings on
physical examination and objective testing and their clinical course often drastically
improves with NSAIDs. Osteomyelitis of the femoral neck, often a precursor to septic
arthritis, may stand as its own entity and is associated with clinical findings similar to
those of hip septic arthritis. Abscess, whether subperiosteal or within a muscle sheath,
and pyomyositis may be associated with similar presentations. A patient with a psoas
abscess will have a clinical examination with more pronounced pain on hip extension
than on internal and external rotation. Patients with obturator pyomyositis also may
have a similar presentation, with the abscess located adjacent to but not within the hip
joint capsule. This differential diagnosis is important to consider because it may affect
the method by which the hip is aspirated9 All of these infectious processes can be
further elucidated via ultrasonography and MRI.10 Tumor of bony structures, such as the

accompanied by infectious laboratory findings. Developmental hip conditions, including
slipped epiphyses and Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease, and fractures about the hip also
should be considered in the differential diagnosis and may be observed on radiographs
and MRIs. Other oncologic pathologies, such as leukemia, may present with
musculoskeletal joint pain and anemia. Rheumatologic processes, such as juvenile
rheumatoid arthritis, and monoarticular arthralgias, such as Lyme arthritis, may be
associated with confusing clinical pictures with elevated laboratory values. Patients may
have large effusions but can better tolerate short arc movements and may not have
fever.11 On diagnosis, these arthropathies generally are managed medically. Non-
orthopaedic intra-abdominal pathology, including appendicitis, ovarian cysts, and
hernias, also may present as hip pain12 (Table 2; Figures 4, 5, and 6).

Diagnostic Testing
Blood tests include complete blood cell count, erythrocyte sedimentation rate (ESR), C-reactive
protein (CRP) level, and blood cultures.
Modified Kocher criteria = white blood cell count greater than 12,000 cells/μL, ESR greater than
40 mm/h, temperature higher than 101.3°F (>38.5°C), inability to bear weight, CRP level greater
than 2.0 mg/dL
Arthrocentesis to include laboratory evaluation of total nucleated cell count, Gram stain, and
culture
Consider septic arthritis if arthrocentesis yields a total nucleated cell count greater than 50,000
cells, 75% neutrophils, positive Gram stain or culture
Radiography, ultrasonography, MRI to evaluate for adjacent pathology

Diagnostic Testing
Concern for septic arthritis should be met with early laboratory and imaging studies.
Given the potential devastating outcomes and broad differential diagnosis, having all the
appropriate information may help lead to correct diagnosis and management. Blood
tests should include blood cultures, a complete blood cell count, CRP level, and ESR.
Lyme titers evaluating immunoglobulin M and immunoglobulin G are essential in
patients in endemic areas. These studies are markers of inflammation and aid in
assessing the systemic reaction of a child to a disease process. Landmark studies in
pediatric orthopaedics have built criteria for the evaluation of septic arthritis using
serum markers of inflammation. The Kocher study used four criteria for the evaluation
of septic arthritis of the pediatric hip versus transient synovitis: peripheral white blood
cell count greater than12,000 cells/μL, ESR greater than40 mm/h, fever higher than
101.3°F (>38.5°C), and inability to bear weight. These criteria were later modified to
include a CRP level greater than 2.0 mg/dL(Table 3). The presence of none of the criteria
in the original study by Kocher et al13 indicated a 0.2% likelihood of septic arthritis, the
presence of one of the criteria indicated a 3% likelihood of septic arthritis, the presence
of two of the criteria indicated a 40% likelihood of septic arthritis., the presence of three
of the criteria indicated a 93.1% likelihood of septic arthritis., and the presence of all four
criteria indicated a 99.6% likelihood of septic arthritis. Temperature was the greatest
single predictor of septic arthritis in the study. Although the study and criteria were

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001052
14/25

designed for septic arthritis of the hip, the laboratory values often are applied to other
joints despite data suggesting that they are not as reliable.14 Arthrocentesis has been
considered a preferred study for the diagnosis of septic arthritis because no serum
marker or imaging study is able to do so. Aspirated synovial fluid should be analyzed for
total nucleated cell count and Gram stain, culture, and the presence of crystals. Glucose
levels and lactic acid also may aid in determining the presence of bacteria.
Unfortunately, some studies have shown that synovial fluid cultures yield positive
bacterial isolates in only 35% of patients.15 Polymerase chain reaction has been used to
identify specific pathogens that are not easily cultured and has led to an increased
incidence of K kingae septic arthritis. A total nucleated cell count greater than 50,000
cells and 75% neutrophils, despite a negative Gram stain and culture, generally is used
as a marker for septic arthritis and, therefore, an indication for surgical management.
Additional studies are actively being performed with basic science laboratory testing to
better isolate pathogens and immunologic markers specific to septic arthritis.

Imaging studies also may play a role in the diagnosis of septic arthritis and should be
included in the workup. Radiographs of the affected limb and joint may demonstrate
joint widening and bony changes associated with effusion and osteomyelitis and other
bony abnormalities. Ultrasonography may be useful in determining the presence of an
effusion. MRI is extremely useful because it may help evaluate for associated pathologies
that also may require management, including osteomyelitis and abscess. MRI should be
used judiciously because it often requires sedation in younger children. Advanced
imaging studies should always be considered in a toxic-appearing child with a clinical
picture for septic arthritis who has normal arthrocentesis results.
Some studies have recommended a protocol for pediatric septic arthritis of the hip in
which MRI with sedation is performed in combination with hip arthrocentesis. This
allows for diagnosis of septic arthritis and assessment for adjacent potential sources of
elevated inflammatory markers.16 Such protocols have shown success in improved time
to management of the infectious etiology and shortened hospital admissions (Figures
7 and 8).Previous studies reported that T1-weighted, T2-weighted fat-saturated, and
short tau inversion recovery MRI techniques are associated with sensitivity and
specificity similar to that of contrast-enhanced MRI techniques, arguing against the need
for and potential morbidity associated with contrast-dependent studies.17

Surgical management with joint capsule incision and drainage is the standard of care for
pediatric septic arthritis.
Trending of CRP levels is the best predictor of treatment response and the need for repeated
treatment.
Empiric antibiotic agents should be initiated immediately after obtaining blood cultures and
tailored based on blood, aspiration, and surgical culture results.
Antibiotic treatment regimen and duration vary

Management
As soon as septic arthritis is deemed likely, blood cultures should be obtained and
empiric antibiotics initiated. Studies show that the initiation of antibiotic agents before
synovial fluid aspiration does not affect culture results.18 Surgical management is
recommended if a high suspicion for septic arthritis exists based on clinical and
laboratory evaluation. Surgical management consists of formal open arthrotomy in
combination with débridement and lavage or arthroscopic debridement. Standard
surgical approaches generally are recommended for all involved joints. The hip joint can
be accessed via an anterior (Smith-Peterson) or medial approach to allow for
capsulotomy and drainage while avoiding disruption of the vasculature of the femoral
epiphysis. Synovial fluid should be sent for further culture to guide antibiotic treatment.
Complete decompression of the joint is important to limit the risk of repeated
accumulation. Many studies recommend leaving the joint capsule open along with the
routine placement of a drain in the joint to allow for further decompression and
prevention of repeated accumulation.Many studies recommend leaving the joint capsule
open along with the routine placement of a drain in the joint to allow for further
decompression and prevention of repeated accumulation. Other studies have advocated
for a partial capsulectomy to ensure that the joint cannot be resealed. Arthroscopic
débridement is safe and effective, with minimal soft-tissue disruption. This surgical
modality often is dictated by surgeon comfort level and the size of the patient.19
Patients must be monitored after surgical treatment to ensure appropriate response.
CRP level has been shown to be the best indicator of treatment response because it
rapidly decreases after adequate management and correlates with clinical
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 6:08 PM
AAOS | Septic Arthritis
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001052
18/25

evaluation.20 An increase in or a persistently elevated CRP level may be an indicator of
repeated accumulation, inadequate decompression, or the presence of other locations
of infection that also may require surgical management. Repeated irrigation and
débridement or additional workup via advanced imaging studies is recommended.
Antibiotic treatment is a requirement in the management of septic arthritis. Antibiotic
therapy is critical in the eradication of the offending organism and supplements surgical
débridement. Historically, the initiation of antibiotic agents was withheld until aspiration
or intraoperative cultures were obtained; however, recent studies have demonstrated
the benefit of immediate, broad-spectrum or anti-staphylococcal antibiotic management
initiated on initial clinical concern without resulting in loss of positive culture rates.
Synovial fluid and tissue cultures should then guide, if necessary, appropriate
modification of antibiotic agents. Intravenous antibiotic administration is the standard of
care, and many studies have cautioned against the early transition to an oral regimen
without a steady clinical improvement. A high-dose oral antibiotic regimen generally can
be adopted after clinical and laboratory improvement is observed over a 4-day period.
Antibiotic therapy traditionally has been successful with a 2- to 3-week course of
organism-specific antibiotic agents for isolated septic arthritis and a 4- to 8-week course
of treatment with associated osteomyelitis or concomitant infection.21 Selection of an
antibiotic agent, the route of administration, and the duration of management should be
based on a team approach, including the orthopaedist and the pharmacist.
Outcomes
Sequelae of septic arthritis include osteonecrosis, chondrolysis, growth disturbance, joint
deformity, hip dislocation, limb-length discrepancy, and malalignment.
Patients should be monitored yearly to evaluate for potential sequelae.

Outcomes
The threshold for surgical management and initiation of antibiotic agents should be
relatively low for the orthopaedic surgeon given the potential complications that may

occur with missed or delayed management of pediatric septic arthritis. Even with timely
management, a risk of long-term sequelae exists, and this must be addressed with
caregivers. The primary goal in the management of septic arthritis is to avoid joint
destruction and osteonecrosis and, therefore, decrease the risk of early arthritis.22 The
hip is especially susceptible to osteonecrosis of the head, proximal femur growth
disturbance, and chondrolysis. Growth disturbance may occur because the physis
frequently is involved, creating the potential for bar formation and epiphysiodesis.23
Therefore, patients must be followed postoperatively to evaluate for any abnormal bone
or joint development. Yearly follow-up may help identify subsequent sequelae and
provide the opportunity to intervene. Some studies have reported that following a
patient to skeletal maturity may not be necessary. Radiographs of the affected joint can
be obtained months after the infection and compared with those of the contralateral
side. The presence of growth arrest lines (Harris lines) may indicate potential growth
disturbance, whereas the absence of growth arrest lines may reassure the surgeon and
family that no long-term sequelae of the infection that will impact growth will occur
(Figure 9; Video 1).
